summary: We built a web-platform that includes (3D Games, mini-arcade games, Ai agent to answer questions, comics & storybooks), we maximized the entertainment goal among each of these modules, to match young kids interests and make the experience fun & educational.
details:
Red Relics: Explore Mars and meet the forgotten machines

What it does and how it works:

Red Relics is a free browser experience where Mars is the menu. You land on a 3D cartoon Mars after a short animated cutscene, and every region you can click is a different way to learn about the robots NASA has left on Mars and the Moon. Memorial Sites tell each machine’s story. The Tales Library holds audio stories, and the Archive has a quiz, a timeline and a short survey. Rober, an AI robot buddy, answers questions using only our verified mission facts.

There are also seven games in total. Six Minigames distributed across six different sites on mars, as well as three comics on three sites, the mini games are:

- Radar Dig: find buried landing hardware with a ground-penetrating radar.

- Moonshot Landing: land on the Moon with engines only, then explore the Apollo sites.

- Signal Delay Drive: plan a rover’s whole day, send it across a signal delay and watch what really happens.

- Rover Workshop: build a rover for a real mission under mass and power limits, then field-test it.

- Dust Storm Survival: keep a solar rover alive through the storms and dust that ended real missions.

- Sojourner: Experience the mission Sojourner did on mars and learn more about the history and last connection it had with Earth

The comics plots were wrote by team members then generated with the help of Nano Banana.

The Garage is a larger game where you build a rover, scan for pieces of old rovers, repair them and use them on your own rover. Repairing a relic unlocks its story in the Library.

Benefits and intended impact:

School-age and casual space fans usually hear only about active missions. Red Relics gives retired and lost machines a voice, and each mini-game links the engineering to the science it made possible. The goal is for players to leave feeling a personal connection to these robots and to understand why they were built the way they were, for example why rovers can’t be steered live, why dust storms ended missions, and why Mars rovers use rocker-bogie wheels. Every game has three difficulty levels, so it works for a child’s first visit and for teens who want a challenge. All spoken lines are also on screen as text, and sound can be muted.

Tools and technology:

- Code: plain JavaScript (ES modules), HTML and CSS. There is no build step.

- 3D: Three.js for the Mars hub [and for the Garage, with Rapier physics].

- Games and art: HTML Canvas and SVG. All icons, buildings, rovers and cutscene art are drawn in code, so there are no image files to download.

- Audio: the Web Audio API [plus ElevenLabs for the voice lines and sound effects].

- AI: Google Gemini powers Rober through a Cloudflare Pages Function, so the API key stays private.

- Hosting: Cloudflare Pages on the free tier. Progress is saved in the browser’s localStorage and there are no accounts.

- Testing: Node scripts with jsdom, plus simulated bot players to tune difficulty.

- AI-assisted development: we used an AI assistant (Claude) to help write code and documentation, and the team reviewed and tested the results.

What’s creative about it

- The whole planet is the menu. Rovers, landers and the Arcade appear as hand-drawn buildings, and routes link them like paths on a map.

- Each game is built on a real operational idea rather than a quiz. For example, in Signal Delay Drive the rover works alone while the signal travels, and in the Dust Storm game you can’t see the rover’s true state unless you spend energy to check on it.

- Real stories drive the gameplay: Opportunity’s 2018 storm, Spirit stuck in soft sand, and InSight’s dust-covered panels. Each ends with a “what really happened” card.

Factors we considered

- Accuracy: every fact has a source and we flag anything simplified. Game numbers like mass, power and energy are game units, not real kilograms or watts.

- Age and accessibility: kid-friendly art, no violence, subtitles for all voice, a mute button, keyboard controls, difficulty levels and a reduced-motion setting.

- Cost and reach: free hosting, small files, no installs, and everything runs in a browser.

- Performance: the hub is built to run on mid-range laptops and phones, and each game cleans up after itself.

- Safety: no accounts or personal data are collected.
